review:
The main strength of the campaigns of Crysis is their sandbox, unrestricted nature, and Crysis 2 is a step back from Crysis 1 and Warhead in this regard, as you run through cities with closed-in walls instead of trek through jungles. However, each specific battle (and there were many times I felt like I was facing "boss" enemies) takes place in a pretty large area, so I never felt particularly restricted.

The guns and combat are as crisp and satisfying as they were in the first two Crysis games. 

The suit's powers are now accessed with keyboard shortcuts, which makes their use feel more isolated, like sprinting in other games, and power jumps are accessed with a single button (holding down space), instead of requiring an activation of strength mode, making me feel less like I was operating a special suit, and more like I was just a superhero - it's less mechanical-feeling, for better or for worse, I guess.

Towards the end of the campaign, I became extremely dependent on cloaking, which is overpowered. It's much faster to sneak around the enemy strongholds, going straight for the objectives, than it is to run roughshod over every enemy one-by-one. Maybe I became so objective-oriented because I was enthralled with the campaign (wishing to finish it as soon as possible), because, in other games, I generally take the time to kill every enemy I see.

My most significant complaint about Crysis 2 is that, with the closed-in areas, specific, restricted routes are required to arrive at objectives within each mission, but there is no guide system (line on the ground) to show you where to go, which would have been appreciated at several points in the campaign, as I found myself trapped in rooms, going in circles trying to open doors that wouldn't budge. If you get stuck and resort to searching online for a level guide, you'll find many other people commenting that they were stuck at the same point as you.

Dying can set you back annoyingly far. Don't die.

The suit's upgradability is neat, but generally not integral, and unlikely to scope an individual's tactics.

There aren't a lot of people playing Crysis 2's multiplayer, although there are more than enough to have a few big games going at all times. Still, this is a game to be bought for its campaign, and I highly doubt you will be left disappointed after completing it. It's exciting, engaging, and challenging, and ranks among my favorite 10-11 hour spans of gaming.

Probably the best Crysis game. The story is pretty ok, and the soundtrack is top notch. Gives me constant adrenaline everytime I encounter the enemies. But don't get me wrong - the game's pretty hard if you don't know what you're doing. Play the game on the Post-Human Warrior difficulty - it's the only way to experience the true challenge that the game offers, along with planning your tactics right ahead for the next encounters. Graphics was way ahead of it's time, CryEngine had some limitations, but it was definitely a beast back then. The graphics is amazing. It looks surreal - and with the Battlefield 3™ destructive environment, it feels alive. It's Crysis 1's graphics style, but in a movie. It doesn't feel realistic, but rather feels like a movie. Like damn, I feel like I'm in an action movie, rather than a FPS game. In a good way.

[h1]Action packed and beautiful to look at, but too linear for its own good.[/h1]

[i]Crysis 2[/i] was developed by Crytek Studios and released by Electronic Arts in March 2011. Four yours earlier, the same developers scored a huge success with the first game in the series, which was well-known at its time of release to be the most demanding pc game ever made. But apart from being a technical masterpiece, pushing graphics to a lever far beyond anything which had been yet achieved, the original [i]Crysis[/i] also offered good gunplay in a fairly big theater of operations. While not being without some problems, the game impressed me and so I started playing [i]Crysis 2[/i] with high expectations.

And that's probably exactly where the problems started: from the beginning, I compared this game to its predecessor. And so I expected a gorgeous looking, extremely demanding shooter within a rather open world, allowing for several routes to achieving one's objectives. [i]Crysis 2[/i] definitely managed to impress me on the visual and technical side: visually it offers anything one could wish for, taking into account the game was released over five years ago. The setting has completely shifted from the lush jungle of the first game to an impressive rendering of New York devastated by war. Although visually still impressive, with tons of details and lots of smoke and debris, the urban setting does diminish the large-scale feeling of the first game quite dramatically, and the different levels felt more constricted and definitely a lot smaller.

From a purely technical point of view, this game still stands firm, although it does show that it was a console port, rather than a game originally developed for pc. The controls are less fluid and intuitive, and seem geared towards playing with an xbox controller. This was actually the first first-person shooter I've ever played with my controller – normally, I definitely prefer keyboard and mouse in this type of games. But in this case, it simply offered better and more naturally laid out controls. As far as graphical settings go – often a problem with a game first developed for consoles: they were fine, offering enough possibilites to crank up the eye-candy to stunning levels and giving (just) enough options to scale the settings for those wanting to do so. It's not the most demanding game out there anymore, but it still can tax any medium-range system: don't expect it to run at full HD on the ultra preset with anything less than a recent, fast i3 and a good midrange gpu. Given the fact that the game has been used so often as a benchmark for computer systems and graphics cards, I was slightly disappointed not to find some sort if benchmarking tool included, but that's a very minor issue.

Much more problematic is the complete transformation as far as the actual gameplay goes. Gone are the open areas where there are several, often radically different, routes to one's objectives. Instead, [i]Crysis 2[/i] offers a series of set pieces: medium-scaled area's with primary and (sometimes) secondary objectives with one or two lines of approach. By using the "tactical mode" of your high-tech suit (more about this in a minute), you can scan the battlefield for enemies, supply stashes, but also for "tactical options", such as the ideal route if going for a stealth approach or the way to go if you want to flank the enemy. In other words: the game wants to hold you by the hand as much as possible! While this might be ok in a very linear first-person horror game, where scripted sequences are of the essence, it is in no way desired in a first-person shooter. I often tried to ignore the tactical suggestions, but mostly found out that there were no viable alternative routes, or that another approach than the one suggested almost inevitably resulted in a quick death. And with its horrendous system of saving only at set (and very irregular) waypoints, dying is something you definitely want to avoid in this game.

Fortunately, not all is bad: the story definitely kept my interest throughout the game and often made me persist through a difficult section. It's not a great story – there are a lot of unbelievable plot-twists and too often a mission ends rahter abruptly – but it's better than in most "super human rescues the world from bad guys and aliens"-games. The most interesting aspect of the game is actually the special combat suit (the nanosuit) which you use as the player throughout the game. Just like in the original [i]Crysis[/i] this suit offers several modes of operation: strength, armor & cloak – the last one of course ideal for a stealth-approach. Since I like being stealthy, the cloak-mode turned out to be my best friend, but it's also a tad overpowered if used correctly. The nanosuit can be upgraded during the game with energy provided by killing aliens, but those upgrades often felt tucked-on and didn't offer anything really new.

As far as the actual gunplay goes, [i]Crysis 2[/i] surely delivers big time. There are a lot of different, often high-tech weapons out there to try out, and after some playing around with them they proved to be very well balanced and offering more than enough firepower for any chosen playstyle. Especially the energy-based weapons, ideal for mowing down aliens, were great fun to use. In the end, I did enjoy this game, if taken on its own merits: I sneaked up on several guards from behind, killed them with my knife, dashed for cover when I ran out of energy for the cloak mode only to be discovered by an alien who then started to throw emp-grenades at me. Very often I could just hang on in a firefight, having to make split-second decisions in order to survive; at other points, I could move forward at leisure, popping in and out of cloak mode. It was great fun, but it wasn't a gaming experience which I'll remember for years to come.

[b]Cautiously recommended: don't compare it to the original game, but enjoy it as a decent first-person shooter. And crank up the volume: the music is fantastic.[/b]

Crysis 2, like the original is a first person shooter. The game was released in early 2011. It also follows on from the plot of Crysis 1 as well. Although you don't really need to have played the original in order to follow the story. Crysis 2 was also the first game to use the CryEngine 3.

The game play has all of the regular FPS style features. You play the role of a Recon Marine, called Alcatraz. You are able to customize your weapons to match the situations you are in, as well as customizing your suite to the same too. Crysis 2 is set in New York City, which is often referred to by many as an urban jungle. This does however offer various different tactical options when it comes to planning attacks; allowing players to navigate between floors and buildings, and ruined buildings.  

We also see a few changes in the Nanosuit used by our character too; this time you are able to use more than one suit power at a time, the strength and power modes have been combined into the same mode, and the stealth suit has been improved slightly.

Crysis 2 has AMAZING graphics; this could easily pass as a game being released recently. If you put all of your settings up to full, you are going to be in amazement at how good this game looks. You will need a beefy rig to keep a steady 60 fps, but my oh my it is worth it.

I sadly see no replay-ability in Crysis 2, there are the addition of a couple of difficulty modes, but to be honest; once you have played it the once, there is no reason to play it again. The single-player campaign is a decent length though - we are looking at a 18 hour long story mode which is very good for an FPS.

Thankfully I had no technical issues with Crysis 2 (unlike I did have with the original), I was able to play with every graphical setting on ultra and still had 60 frames the whole time. The only thing I will mention is there is no longer any multiplayer support since GameSpy shut it's servers down in May 2014.

If you enjoyed the first Crysis game, you will basically enjoy Crysis 2, it's the same just with even better graphics, more compelling story, and stellar FPS action and did I mention the amazing graphics? People may think £20 is a bit steep for a game of this age, however I am completely happy with this price as it almost fits into the £1/hour ratio.

[h1] This isn't a war ordinary humans can win! This is the future! [/h1]
I still remember being very hyped after watching Crysis 2 trailers and promotional material. I was all in when Crytek decided to expand the series outside the Lingshan islands we last saw in the original Crysis and its spinoff Warhead. I’m going to be as honest and unbiased with you guys as possible. Despite being a huge fan of the series as whole, I wasn’t very impressed with the sequel. It almost felt like developer Crytek was trying to make a much bigger and ambitious sequel to an already great phenomenon.   

[h1]Pros[/h1]
+Visually stunning and absolutely breathtaking. Crysis 2 showcases massive amounts of action set-pieces and Hollywood level of destruction. Playing this in 2011 on PC at max settings must have been every fan’s dream. 
+Built on Crytek’s heavily modified Cryengine 3. The developers have pushed graphics to it’s absolute limits. Fine tuned and well optimized and also runs much better than the original. You could almost call it very expensive interactive tech demo. It’s a wonder this game came out in 2011. 
+Combat feels smooth and crisp. 
+Expanded weapon selection and upgrades
+The amount of detail put into Manhattan streets and is absolutely stunning. 
+Epic soundtrack. Shoutout to EA for bringing in the “legendary” Hans Zimmer to compose the main title sequence. You can play the soundtrack through the main menu as well. 
+Clean and modern HUD & UI.
+Using Nano suit feels much easier than it did in Crysis. You activate armor and stealth modes on the Q and E keys (by default).

[h1]Cons[/h1]
-The overarching level design is far more linear compared the first game. This is a huge step back from the original Crysis as that game gave a lot of freedom to explore lush forestry areas and lush mountains and use alternate paths. This isn’t the case with most missions you get in Crysis 2. Concept was pretty solid as shown in the trailers but very poorly executed in the final game. 
-Lacks a good compelling villain. General Kyong was a bit goofy in the first game but at least he had a realistic motivation and a sense of personality. In this game your main target is to fight the aliens or save an already destroyed Manhattan from something?  
-Mediocre plot. It’s one of the most forgettable stories Crytek came up with as an excuse to shift the focus on urban setting. Even the comics had far better story to tell imo. 
-No side missions or optional objectives.
-Some aliens felt like bullet sponges, not sure if this was because I chose a higher difficulty.
-Yet another mute protagonist with no personality and background. 
-I’ll be honest, this game has a very forgettable cast of characters. The first Crysis had memorable characters such as Nomad, Psycho, Korean General Kyong, Dr. Rosenthal and finally Prophet. Sadly none of the people really matter in Crysis 2, I’m serious!
-There are a lot of unbelievable plot twists and too often a mission ends rather abruptly which brings me to Crysis 2’s ending. It has to be of the most disappointing final levels/endings according to me.
-No FOV slider. No way to change/override default field-of-view. Trying to tinker with config file always resets after every level/cutscene/restart.  
-Boring pre-rendered cutscenes showing your GPS location from one part of Manhattan to other. 
-Dumb enemy A.I even on hard difficulty setting. It could really detract you from the excitement.
-Strangely, the aliens look nothing like the ones Nomad and his unit fought in the first game.
-Multiplayer has been dead since 2014 following the closure of GameSpy. 
-Quick saving is replaced by checkpoint autosaves.
-Few technical glitches and bugs. 
-No quality of life features such as achievements, cloud support, local co-op multiplayer. 
-Despite a solid mod support most Cryengine 3 mods have been abandoned.
-No achievements, cloud support, trading cards or local co-op modes.
-As of June 2020, EA recently removed/delisted Crysis collection bundle off Steam which included Crysis 1, Warhead at lower price and increased prices in nearly every country except United States. 

[h1]The Bottom Line[/h1]
If you enjoy first-person sci-fi shooters and want a visually stunning experience, then with no doubt go for it. It’s clear they spent big money on this project with EA being attached as funding partner and publisher. It’s fun as long as you don’t take the plot seriously. Play it like you’re watching a Transformers movie and you won’t regret buying this game if you’re looking for a solid fun and action shooter!
If you haven’t played Crysis 2 yet and plan to do so then please get it on sale, if you were able to stay away from this game until now, wait for it. Get it for $10 or less, nothing more. The multiplayer has been dead since ages.  
For those who are wondering what does the Maximum Edition add to the single player, the answer may not be really that exciting as the name implies because, in terms of content pretty much nothing was really added however this is the fully patched, definitive version with high quality texture pack pre-installed. The story of Crysis 2 takes place couple of years after a limited 6 issue tie-in comic book volume published by IDW Comics. The comics explains Nomad’s journey after the first game and foreshadows how Prophet and Hargreaves fit into the Manhattan story. Maybe check that out if you can!

It’s hard not to miss the more open ended approach of the first game, and the nerfed abilities make the shift even more noticeable. This one takes a more grounded approach in its narrative, gameplay, and environmental design. It’s without a doubt “consolized,” but that’s not necessarily a bad thing it’s just a bit jarring coming straight from the first. That said, the improved alien design is a huge plus. In the first game, they felt more like a nuisance than anything truly threatening, but here they’re faster, more aggressive, and actually intimidating. I genuinely enjoy fighting them this time around. Visually, it still holds up incredibly well it impressed me then and it still does now, which says a lot. Overall its just a good game, I miss the format of older games a short but fun campaign and solid multiplayer to go with it, not a year investement, a list of to do chores, and stringing me along with predatory market practices.

To be honest, I never liked Crysis. I always looked at it as a techdemo. It was one of those games that had numerous glitches - BSODs and audio glitches were frequent and I do not remember any other games with which I was having similar issues at the time. Also, my rig surpassed the system requirements for the game so I never understood what could have caused these issues. But the various websites and forums on the internet confirmed the same.

In any case, the jungle environment was already familiar following Crytek's Far Cry. So, when the news came that the sequel to Crysis would take place in New York (now an "urban jungle"), I looked forward to seeing and playing it. The game delivered: the destroyed cityscape of Manhattan looks superb thanks to CryEngine 3. We are to navigate between the floors of destroyed buildings and combat on the city streets is common. Finally, the aliens appear in the form of regular soldiers, too - it's not just the big monsters that you need to fight like in the first part.

As for gameplay, the protagonist's nano suit has been streamlined. Strength and speed modes are now combined. We can now perform silent takedowns so following a stealthy playing mode is more rewarding. Upgrading the suit's features is a possibility based on the alien kills we perform - this is an unnecessary role playing section of the game but it does not represent any issues.

Overall, I was satisfied with the sequel. Single player campaign lasts for 12-13 hours which is quite long these days. Cutscenes are frequent and Hans Zimmer's excellent score helps us with the immersion into the world of Crysis. Too bad that starting from June multiplayer mode will be unavailable for good (following the announcement of GameSpy), so, should it be discounted, it should be purchased with only the single player experience in mind.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]Crysis 2[/b] is a linear first-person shooter developer by [i]Crytek[/i], and sequel to [i]Crysis 1[/i], narrating the struggle of Alcatraz, the [b]only survivor of a marine commando[/b] sent to New York City, devastated by an alien invasion, in order to extract a high priority target. After [b]acquiring the iconic Nanosuit[/b], players will face both human and alien enemies in a desperate attempt to save Manhattan. 

Other than visuals, which are [b]absolutely impressive even nearly a decade after release[/b], Crysis 2 also offers [b]quality action, with multiple approaches to most enemy encounters[/b], varied enough weaponry with customization options, suit powers such as invisibility, armor and super-speed, and upgrade trees for each of them. Enemy types are [b]not so varied, totaling just 3 for human CELL forces and 5 for alien troops, which becomes a bit stale in the long run[/b], excluding special bosses such as gunships. Being an action-focused experience, there [b]won't be much else besides combat except some collectibles to find, few longer cut-scenes and some brief exploration segments[/b]. The variety of approaches proposed keeps the gameplay fresh enough throughout the experience.

This game also has some problems: [b]first of all, the DX11 enhanced graphics mode does not work properly on Win8/10[/b]. Secondly, [b]some weapons and suit upgrades are OP[/b], (Grendel, Deflection...) with players ending up using / spamming those all the time instead of having more variety, while [b]many other weapons and suit upgrades are gimmicky or useless[/b] throughout the whole game. Last thing, [b]enemy AI is inconsistent[/b], performing quality maneuvers at times while just getting stuck in clusters doing nothing, or coming one at a time to their death in a brainless fashion in others.

Overall, [b]Crysis 2[/b] is a [b]solid FPS capable of delivering satisfying action, gunplay and challenge at higher difficulties[/b], not without its problems, which in the end do not prevent it from being a worthy sequel. [b]Priced at 20€ default, and offering about 6-8 hours of content depending on difficulty without much replay value but also overall good quality, I can suggest getting it at full price for FPS fans or those who already played Crysis 1, while others could wait for a sale, since this game gets discounted heavily pretty often.[/b]

[h1]Pros & Cons[/h1]

🔵 [b]Pros[/b]
+ Incredible graphics, managing to compete nearly on-par with current releases, despite being almost 10 years old.
+ Satisfying combat with solid gun feeling, varied approach possibilities and good challenge on higher difficulties.
+ Customization options and suit upgrades give more needed depth to the basic FPS gameplay.

🔴 [b]Cons[/b]
- DirectX11 graphics enhancements do not work properly on Win8/10, forcing to use DX9 instead.

- Some weapons and suit upgrades are too good, while many others are gimmicky or useless. 
- Environmental destruction, physics took a big step back compared to Crysis 1.

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]

🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
The gameplay of [b]Crysis 2[/b] is divided into Exploration, Customization and Combat.

[b]Exploration[/b] is pretty linear since the levels are not very open. Mostly, exploring will consist in looking for ammo caches to resupply weapons or acquire better ones, or getting to a Tactical Point previously scouted using the visor, which highlights various tactical advantages before a big fight on the map. The presence of collectibles is something that makes exploring a bit more worthwhile for those interested in additional lore or completionists, but they add nothing practical to the gameplay. Overall the exploration in Crysis 2 is pretty limited and only a few areas open up a bit more, but still is an integral part of the gameplay to find resources or the best route of attack.

[b]Customization[/b] goes twofold: first, all weapons can be customized with previously found attachments, meaning that to unlock more you need to fist find them on enemy weapons. These attachments can impact significantly how a weapon works, giving it more power, flexibility or other features you may need to approach a specific section, including silencers, grenade launchers and optical scopes. The second part of customization is about the suit, upgraded with Nanotech gained from enemy alien corpses; the fact dropped Nano disappears over time encourages a more direct, fast approach in fighting aliens. Suit upgrades enhance stealth, armor, speed and tracking abilities - only one upgrade can be active for each power, and while some such as Deflection are a must, many others are gimmicky without being real worth the Nano price asked. 

[b]Combat[/b] is the true core of Crysis 2, and plays out in a realistic manner with a very satisfying feel to it, especially regarding hit feedback, gun feeling and explosions / destruction on the field, with tons of physics-based objects flying around, as well enemy corpses, not as much as in Crysis 1 perhaps, but still noteworthy. The main feature about combat here is that there are several approaches to a single fight: detaching a heavy machine gun from a truck using it to plow your way through enemies, or instead stealth killing from the distance with a sniper rifle, or again avoiding the fight altogether by finding a path, are all viable methods. The combat challenge, on Hard and Posthuman is considerable, though once Deflection is unlocked armor becomes so hard it will considerably lower most enemy threats. Enemies generally hit pretty hard and using powers to your full extent, with an eye on energy consumption, will be invaluable to win. Overall the combat in this game is very engaging and satisfying, FPS fans will surely love it, as I did.

🔩 [b]Performance Analysis[/b]
[u]PC Specs: RTX2080Ti, Ryzen 3900X, 32GB RAM DDR4[/u]
Goes without saying that a medium spec or better config by today's standards is need to run this game well in 1080p or more. As far as optimization goes, the game doesn't have many issues, but the visuals and effects it proposes are very intensive. On this configuration the game ran a solid 90+ FPS in 1440p with maxed out settings,the only problem to report is graphics glitching out a couple times impairing visuals, easily solved by changing resolution and changing it back again. There are no other bugs or issues to report, except the already mentioned DX11 issue.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
[b]Crysis 2[/b] is overall a solid FPS with impressive graphics, satisfying combat and enough variety to keep it interesting until the end. It may have its problems, but it still is a game i would completely suggest to any FPS / Sci-fi fan.

I’m a latecomer to the Crysis franchise. I played Crysis Remastered last year and wasn’t too impressed. The visuals didn’t impress in 2021 and the gameplay and story left a lot to be desired.  So I reluctantly bought Crysis 2 once it hit the magic 75% discount target on Steam that normally gets me to pull the trigger (pun intended) on games I’m sitting on the fence with.
And so far (I’m about two-thirds of the way through the campaign) I’ve been pleasantly surprised.
The game runs flawlessly on Deck and I’ve been able to play with all graphical settings set to Ultimate and the frame rate locked at 30fps. This nets me with about 3hrs of playtime. I went with the standard control scheme and enabled gyroscopic aiming.
The level design and visuals are incredibly impressive on Deck and the level of detail and realism in the levels make me believe this could almost be a new release. You don't have time to read this entire thing do you? Here's my conclusion ahead of time:

CONCLUSION:
Overall Personal Rating: 8/10.
Keep in mind I have not tested multiplayer at all, I have not played Crysis 1 or 3, and I bought this game for 75% off (about $8).  If you want a dated but still kinda relevant, cheesy experience of being a BAMF, just get the game when it's on sale, do it. :) Keep your expectations grounded because this game is over a decade old, prepare to wrestle with technical difficulties like I have listed above, and you'll have a grand time. Personally I recommend playing with a controller if you are originally a console gamer, but keyboard and mouse is just as acceptable, especially if you are used it.

CONS:
Ok, let's start with what's wrong with the game, stick around to the end for pros and keep in mind that I absolutely recommend the game and these are just opinions:
1) First-Time-Boot up Tech Issues: As you may have guessed based on my note above, getting the settings dialed in upon first boot-up is the number one issue for me, took me about 45 mins to an hour to figure out what I just typed above and I almost returned it. The fact that Steam does not have a fix to spare me this kind of frustration is almost unacceptable.
2) Occasionally non-responsive controls: The controls are a bit non-responsive sometimes during gameplay in certain scenarios.  You may be trying to do one action and want to do another at the same time ie. reload, and crouch at the same time, and it only lets you do one or the other if you press the buttons at the same time. Another example is trying to max out armor and stand up at the same time so you can sprint away from danger; armor didn't max out, but I stood up, ended up getting killed.
3) Story, voice acting, and dialogue is a bit mediocre. Don't expect a serious narrative.
4) AI Enemies easy: Enemies are a little too dumb on normal difficulty and aren't very aggressive, but hey.
5) Silencers have no cons, which is a con: in most games, silencers have some sort of drawback whether it's decreased accuracy, limited weapons you can use silencers for, or even limited silencer duration (like Last of Us Part 2), but in this game? Zero drawback to using them, and in my opinion it makes me *too* overpowered. Putting a silencer on a shotgun? I shouldn't be able to do that without sacrificing something gameplay-wise.
6) Extremely linear story: Level progression is similar to COD, and granted if you like that kind of thing, more power to you; I personally got mega addicted and blew through the game in 15 hours so I didn't mind.  The sense of urgency in the story kinda makes the linear nature acceptable for me personally, but I know not everyone likes that so it's worth mentioning. 
7) Nano-vision (thermal/night vision) costs energy: Why does my thermal vision wear out my suit's power? I should have unlimited thermal vision, but instead I have to turn it off every 20 seconds before I run critically low on my suit power and can't use max armor or camo when I need it most. -_- It makes levels in the dark somewhat irritating--forgivable, but irritating. 
8) AI Team Mates are useless: Apparently you have to do every freaking thing yourself. ie. destroying a giant alien walking tank with alien grunts chasing you whilst trying to find explosive ammo to fight the tank off because you ran out of missles. Multiple deaths. When I finally beat this section, all of a sudden I hear Marines yelling in my ear over comms: "Good job! Now get your ass back here, let's go!" I seriously forgot they were even there.  Bitch, where even were you?? 

Pros, and why I recommend the game:
1) Concept is pretty cool: You're a marine with an adaptive nanosuit that you have to wear otherwise you will succumb to pre-existing fatal injuries. Your suit is also evolving on a cellular (or should I say nano-cellular?) level to alien contact, and is the only key to stopping the alien-manufactured disease they are using against humanity.
2) BAMF Factor: You're a pretty strong character in game, especially if you play on normal, and with the upgrades you can get you're able to go full bruiser mode and absorb bullets like a sponge and attack head on, or be practically invisible and use stealth and go HAM with headshots, neck cracks, and back stabs.  The arsenal that you can carry is also ridiculously huge, yet plausible given that your character has super strength and can physically carry it all on his person (even if there's no visible backpack or pockets to stuff your 3 disposable missile launchers, but cut this game some slack it's an old game).
3) Weapon Customization: Oh. My. Gawd. This has to be one of my favorite parts. In real time, you can swap out scopes, silencers, and modular attachments (mini-shotguns/grenade launchers) on certain weapons. Friggin. Cool. No upgrade trees required as far as I've discovered.
4) Stands the test of time: Despite being an older game, the gameplay and graphics are at surprising levels of quality for what you would expect.  Obviously don't go comparing this to Uncharted or God of War because it'll be blown out of the park by them, but as a game, let alone one that's, what, 10 years old or more?, this game is excellent.
5) Stealth: The stealth alone is outstanding if you play correctly. You can survey and tag certain elements in the battlefield like enemies, ammo cashes, and tactical elements like sniper nests before you jump in and they'll stay on screen; and with active camo, a silenced automatic, and a silenced sniper rifle, you are nearly unstoppable and it feels awesome.
6) Morbidity of the alien plague: There are aliens and there is a plague used against the humans as a bio weapon, and seeing the dying civilians and the affect on their bodies, and understanding the designed purpose of this plague by the aliens...it's some brutal stuff, pretty metal.
7) Marines are cool: Honestly, the attitude of the Marines in the game is realistic and pretty dope. I like Marines. Marines scratch my American patriot itch. Completely personal preference.

[h1]Crysis 2[/h1]
The fact is that [b]Crysis 2[/b] (at the time) became a kind of quality indicator. You've probably heard someone talk about a PC with a monstrous configuration, a statement that was usually replied with the following sentence: “But does it run Crysis at maximum?”.

[b]Crysis 2[/b] appeared very different from what many fans expected at the time, leaving aside the entire forest setting and replacing it with skyscrapers and the paved streets of New York. However, that wasn't what scared most of the game's fans the most, but rather the fact that Crysis 2 had become multiplatform at that time.

[b]Certainly, it would have been almost impossible to get the original game to run on seventh generation consoles. Just look at the size of the environment, a gigantic island that provides an open world experience, and you will notice that [b]Crytek[/b] knew how to make the most of what PCs at the time had to offer. It would be physically impossible to port all of Crysis' content onto a dual-layer DVD or Blu-ray.[/b]

Therefore, Crysis 2 had everything to be a more limited game than the first — at least that's what many fans believed. But finally, the work was in our hands. I spent a good few hours with the game and I can safely guarantee that fans of the first game won't be disappointed.

[b]Crysis 2 is phenomenal. Okay, we may not have an environment as geographically impressive as the island of Lingshan, from the first game, but that doesn't mean the New York portrayed in the title fails to take our breath away.[/b]

[b]Crytek[/b] did a great job in the sequence, creating a game that is a true example of cinematography in electronic entertainment. Furthermore, this time we didn't just have beautiful visuals, which easily surpass what was established by the first. Instead, Crysis 2 really decides to consolidate itself as a game in the FPS genre, dedicating its characteristics to the genre and establishing itself as one of the best shooters of this generation. let's play.

Unlike its predecessor, Crysis 2 did not stand out only for its graphic beauty. Instead, the title managed to create a fun formula, improving the details of the first game and bringing new features that every fan of the FPS genre is looking for. All of this accompanied by a cool atmosphere, in a New York that also serves as a structural pillar for the game and an unprecedented alien invasion...

[b]The title's cinematic campaign manages to bring together memorable visuals with gameplay reinforced by the exclusives of Nanosuit 2.0, which gave new air to a much explored genre.[/b]

Even with some minor issues, Crysis 2 has established itself as an intense game in every way, becoming more extraordinary the more you play. After achieving superiority in visuals, the Crysis franchise also rose to first place in fun.

Crysis 2 does an admirable job of living up to the original's reputation of sheer technical prowess, though the visuals aren't as immediately impressive as you may expect. But this sequel still looks great and plays that way too. The jungle is now of the urban variety--New York City to be precise. You make your way through office buildings, across crumbling bridges, and around broad city squares, where robotic aliens infest hallways and swarm across rooftops. Large environments give you room to maneuver and grant you freedom to approach battle in a number of ways, which makes Crysis 2 a great alternative to the plethora of first-person shooters that usher you down corridors on your way to the next action movie set piece.Crysis 2 does an excellent job of portraying a city under siege without indulging in constant action-film cutaways. There is still plenty of cinematic excess here, though it's delivered organically. Yes, there are a few scripted moments in which you are more of an observer than a participant; and, yes, you might be able to hold a button to peer at the imposing alien structure towering in the distance. But rather than wrest control away from you to highlight every falling skyscraper, collapsing passageway, and hovering alien ship, Crysis 2 allows these events to simply happen. And, because they are often so momentous, your attention is drawn to them. The few occasions when the game stops to consider how the average citizen might be affected by an alien invasion lend humanity to your militaristic actions. Familiar landmarks are defaced, lay in ruin, or explode as you watch. There's an eerie contrast between the untouched trees of Central Park swaying in the wind and the rubble stretching behind them. The visual design eschews artistic flair in favor of authenticity, and it mostly succeeds at providing a frightening real-world backdrop for large-scale shoot-outs.You play as a marine known as Alcatraz, and like Nomad in the original game, you are outfitted with a nanosuit. This suit makes you the soldier of the future; it allows you to jump to great heights, temporarily cloak yourself, and scan your environment. You can also activate a mode that boosts your armor. You receive this suit in dramatic fashion from the original game's Prophet, and the nature of this technology figures heavily into the story. Someone wants that suit. Thus, you aren't just fighting off an alien invasion, but you're also fighting ground troops that would be happy to see you dead. You won't find much of interest in the characters, and the meandering plot takes a while to find its rhythm. But once it does, it carries you along properly, delivers a few twists, and comes to an intriguing conclusion that you won't see coming. How refreshing it is for a game to set up a sequel without resorting to cheap cliches.It's a shame that it takes several nondescript hours of FPS action before you get to see the spectacular devastation. In fact, if you haven't played the original Crysis, the first few hours of the sequel might make you wonder why it is so beloved. You spend the early going pitted against relatively dumb human enemies who run past you but fail to shoot, stand around staring straight ahead, and otherwise act as if they don't know you are standing right there pumping them full of lead. The troublesome AI is Crysis 2's most notable flaw, and it often combines with other glitches in bizarre ways. In an early foggy level, you might shoot at a soldier who not only fails to respond to you even though blood is gushing from him each time a bullet finds its mark but also fails to die. You catch friendlies and aliens standing around together, looking like they might be enjoying each other's company. Aliens run into objects and then just run in place rather than go around them or leap over. The AI simply isn't good, and its mediocrity stands out all the more against the otherwise convincing climate.

Crysis 2 set out to take everything that made its predecessor a technical marvel and refine it into a more accessible, fast-paced shooter. 
And while it certainly delivers some thrilling moments and impressive visuals, it doesn’t quite recapture the open-world jungle stealth that made the first game so iconic.
The change in setting from the jungle to an urban environment is a bold shift, but it introduces a more linear structure that feels somewhat restrictive, especially for those who loved the sandbox-style freedom of the first game. 
New York itself is a beautifully detailed war zone, but it’s a far cry from the lush, expansive jungles of Crysis.
One of the standout features of Crysis 2 is, unsurprisingly, its visual fidelity. 
The game is absolutely stunning, with some of the best lighting and detailed textures of its time. 
The city’s towering skyscrapers and desolate streets look phenomenal, with dynamic weather and destruction adding to the immersion. 
If you’re playing it on a capable machine, it’s easy to get lost in the beauty of it all.
The Nanosuit still provides a range of abilities, but this time, combat is much more action-focused. 
The addition of a more streamlined experience, including quicker movements, tight corridors, and intense firefights, turns Crysis 2 into a more traditional first-person shooter. 
While the cloak and armor abilities are still enjoyable, the focus on tighter levels and less open-ended gameplay doesn’t give you the same sense of power or freedom as the first game did. 
The game feels more like a "shoot 'em up" than the strategic, stealth-based experience that Crysis offered.
Combat itself is solid, with well-designed weapons and enemy AI that offers a decent challenge. 
The alien enemies, while interesting and varied, don’t evoke the same awe as the ones in the first game, and their repetitive design often makes encounters feel formulaic. 
The inclusion of human enemies, however, brings a decent level of variety to the action.
Unfortunately, the narrative doesn’t do much to elevate the experience. 
The plot feels like a typical alien invasion story, and the characters, including Alcatraz, are flat and lack the emotional depth that would have made the stakes feel more meaningful.
All in all, Crysis 2 is a game with plenty of technical polish and high-octane action, but it falls short of recapturing the magic of the original. 
The switch to a more linear structure, coupled with a less captivating story, makes it feel more like a solid shooter than the genre-defining experience the first game was.
If you're in it for the action and beautiful visuals, Crysis 2 delivers. 
But if you were hoping for the same kind of immersive, open-world stealth and freedom that made the original such a standout, you may find yourself a bit disappointed.
A visually stunning, action-packed shooter that doesn't quite live up to its predecessor's legacy.

Predator 1 worked because the jungle was the character — tension, isolation, mystery. Predator 2 dragged the Predator into a noisy city full of cops, chaos, and zero atmosphere, killing the vibe. Crysis 2 does the exact same thing: trades wild freedom for urban clutter and calls it “evolution.”

-Feels soulless.
-Crysis didn’t need a city.
-It needed a spine.

Crysis 2 is a first-person post-apocalyptic shooter developed by Crytek Studios and published by Electronic Arts. The game was released in March 2011. The story continues from Crysis 1 where the Ceph invaded the Lingshan Islands into them invading New York, USA. The player plays as Alcatraz, a member of Force Recon One, whose mission to infiltrate and capture Dr. Nathan Gould goes terribly wrong. This review will discuss the campaign and the dialogue, the gameplay and the features, performance and graphics, and the issues with the game. I did not test the multiplayer component as the online portion went offline in 2015. In addition, the Maximum Edition aspect of the game is irrelevant as all of the contents were related to multiplayer.

Crysis 2 encompassed a good and logical storytelling campaign. The story expands on the Ceph invasion into America from the Lingshan Islands and the inevitable counter-attack by the Americans. Furthermore, the game provides great insight into the background of characters that carried before and through both games, notably Prophet and Jacob Hargreave. For instance, Prophet reveals that following Crysis 1, he found out it was not the last of the Ceph, rather the beginning of a new war. The story in the game made sense by the end of the campaign so I commend Crytek for elegantly telling the story. However, I do not like the massive logic gap from Crysis 1 to 2 because the sequel does not mention the aftermath of the cliff-hanger in Crysis 1 as the aftermath is explained through the Crysis comics series, which irritated me and I feel is an unwise business move. But, the dialogue in the campaign was excellent in telling the story. I completed the campaign in 10 hours and my favourite component was the team-based missions alongside the US Marines because many post-apocalyptic games result in a lonely protagonist. My second issue within the campaign was the lack of real excitement in cut scenes that clarified a major part of the overall story. For instance, when Jacob Hargreave reveals his knowledge about the Ceph, which I will not spoil, it comes across as another cut scene, not as a great storytelling moment, even if it was. Lastly, this game features some collecting aspects such as collecting dog tags on missions, collecting flashbacks, and so forth. It's not overly filler but it's not overly interesting to invest the extra time into finding the extras. Overall, the campaign is good because the story within the game, not the overall story is told with depth and precision and has minimal loopholes. The main issue of having to follow the comic series to determine what happened in the cliff-hanger from Crysis 1 does hurt my overall experience of the campaign.

Crysis 2 possesses a variety of gameplay features to mostly improve the game. First, the game features a levelling system in which Alcatraz can kill the Ceph and garner Nano Catalyst points to upgrade his nanosuit. There are four different tiers with three upgrades in each, which is separated into tactical, armour, power, and stealth module tiers. This is a decent system because it allows you to improve Alcatraz's overall combat effectiveness and it has a nice balance to not overpower him but improve him because as the campaign progresses so does the difficulty of the Ceph. My major annoyance with this system was the lack of clarification if an ability is active or not once you purchase it. For instance, if I buy threat tracker, the game does not mention whether its active. The second gameplay feature is the layout of missions in the campaign. I really like the layout of the missions because despite the game being linear, you can approach a mission in a variety of ways. For instance, when Alcatraz opens his visor, he can see his tactical options for the mission, which may be going 100 metres to the right through stealth to complete the mission or going forward 30 metres and grenade the enemy. Furthermore, the weapon customisation system expands on the variety of approaches in a mission because Alcatraz can alter his gun depending on what approach he wants to take, ie. Stealth approach and a silencer. This freshens the gameplay and missions because Alcatraz has various options in completing a mission and can suit his equipment towards that approach. Lastly, the weapon combat, melee system, and vehicle movement and combat are all smooth, fluid and enjoyable. Vehicular combat does spice up the game, particularly on long distance missions. Overall, I commend the gameplay and the variety of features because it all does enhance the game experience.

Crysis 2 has very consistent performance and beautiful graphics. This game reinforces why Crytek were the leaders in gorgeous games because this 2011 game is truly a stunning game. The graphics are superb, from the destruction that affects the landscape to the realism of characters to the overall tone of the post-apocalyptic atmosphere. Furthermore, I like the simplicity of the UI, which is the main menu. The performance as mentioned, is very consistent. On my mid-tier system, which specs are highlighted on my profile page, I played on very high settings and drew a constant 35-50 fps. When there were FPS drops throughout a mission, there was no stuttering, making performance steady throughout a mission. However, at the beginning of the majority of missions there would be a major freeze probably due to a massive fps drop for some unknown reason. Loading times varied in the game. Some missions took longer to load than others, which was annoying on some levels but not a major nuisance. Overall, the only hitch in performance was the start of the mission stuttering, but for the most part this was a smooth game. Likewise, the graphics was top-notch.

Despite most of the review containing positives and some containing negatives, this game had a ton of bugs and glitches. I encountered six bugs and/or glitches that occurred frequently throughout the campaign. For instance, the worst was the sound engine dying, resulting in me restarting my computer. The second worst annoying bug was dialogue showing up on the screen as I had subtitles enabled and the characters that were meant to say those lines went silent, pointing to more issues likely with the sound engine. And the other bugs and glitches was mainly relating to dialogue, event sequences and gameplay. All in all, the issues did hurt the game for me.

Overall, Crysis 2 is a good game that features a logical and competent campaign, great gameplay and features, a beautiful atmosphere and environment and consistent performance for the most part. This game had a deep and logical story that explained the specifics and the broader picture. It provided fluid combat and various approaches to tackling missions, freshening the linear aspect of the game. The main issues was the logic gap from Crysis 1 to Crysis 2 due to the business idea that the story should be advanced through Crysis Comic series and the amount of bugs and glitches infested into it. This game is $29.99 and you can get up to 18 hours in my opinion on the game fitting in the campaign and the extras. At $29.99, I recommend getting this on sale. However, if you are completely new to the series, I recommend getting the Crysis Collection at full price of $44.99 because there is three different games that tell a massive story and all of which have been well received.

Reality 2.0. A review from New York.

There is this morbid fascination with seeing New York destroyed in movies. This game does just that and does it really well.

The graphics.

Nothing to say here. Cry Engine 3 is going to dominate the graphics department until Frostbite 2 comes out I guess. It's going to be an interesting stand off. I did however notice some inconsistencies with water. Most water still looks great. However, some parts of the water are just outright consolish looking. As I was playing the game, I found myself constantly being distracted by the graphics whilst I was getting shot at which was annoying. However, when you are invisible, you still cast a shadow and your floating gun is also visible to the enemy. Now the game gives you the option to run around in third-person view.

The story:

Well, you still play as a mute character named 'Alcatraz'. Nomad actually had a voice. And they do attempt to tie in the story with the first game, somewhat. But hey, on the positive note, you can actually cast a shadow and you have legs this time around.

The locations:

There are 19 missions. You start off at Battery park and then you advance towards the downtown area of the city through the East side. You will visit many historic locations and some of them are going to be blown up. The scale of the buildings in the game and reality is almost 1:1. One thing is that the skyscrapers in the background are randomly picked. Apparently the devs did not wish to go through more trouble of placing the real skyscrapers in the corresponding locations. Let's get one thing straight. This is not a sandbox game. At the end of the day, you are given an area that you have to navigate through to get to the next check point. So even though that makes the game linear, the fact that there are several approaches to your destination kind of makes the city your playground. I loved seeing the old closed off Brooklyn Bridge 6 train subway stop. They have only recently re-opened it by the way.
The NYC subway maps that are in the game are wrong though, not to mention some geographical errors. The devs also put the train tracks on the streets, and NYC does not have those except for the old abandoned old track that was delivering coal to a plant a hundred years ago; now it is a museum.
But at least the intersecting streets and historical locations are correct.
The game does give you a significant area to run around when you approach the Grand Central terminal, otherwise the entire game consists of isolated carefully constrained few blocks that you have to go through.
The bottom line is that, it is not really New York as I hoped to see it, but it is New York enough.
Times Square has been pulled off very well, but of course, most of its blocked up by the mysterious US Army cement blocks, seriously? The US army can barricade NYC in the matter of hours of alien attack with thousands of these blocks?
Hint, when you find the head of the Statue of Liberty, go inside of it.

The sound:

The sound is great. Distant shots, shouts, explosions, alien growls, your gun shots - it's all there. Can't comment on the music however, since it ruins the immersion for me, no music necessary.

The gameplay:

Extremely smooth. Quick load times as usual, responsive keyboard and mouse. The recoil is extremely realistic, unlike other FPS games. Even throwing a grenade is bound to give your screen a shake. They slightly augmented the role of the nano suit here. This time, the energy regenerates much faster. Not only that, the energy regenerates no matter what. So even if you are swimming, your energy will eventually recharge even if you do not surface. Needless to say, that makes the game easier than the first one in that department. There is also a cover system even though I didn't use it a lot. It is reminiscent of the Killzone franchise, wherein you remain in cover and you are able to peek out and see what's going on ahead, instead of being able to see everything if you were playing a third person shooter.
You can still grab the aliens by their throat and choose to either knife them, throw them or use them for cover. But you can't just take any alien by its throat. You have to either soften the alien and pump it full of lead first or punch it a few times, then you have the option to grab the poor bastard.
Sliding. Not really that useful but it's nice to have the ability.
The ability to climb up if you just can't reach that ledge. I found myself jumping from building to building just to grab onto the ledge and pull myself up.
The strong kick. Useful in kicking large things around.
You can upgrade your suit and your weapons based on your progress in the game and how many enemies you killed.
Introducing the nano vision. No more night vision. This time, you can see traces of water vapor or traces of heat or enemies while everything else on the screen remains black and white.
The game gives you the option to bypass your enemies completely, and most of the time you can pull that off.
There is some driving, but it only last a few seconds at a time.

The ammo caches are scattered throughout the city. So even though you cannot carry as much ammo at a time, you will easily find ammo elsewhere.
There are a few types of aliens, but most of them are infantry. You will find some big fat ones and a tripod. You will also see a couple of cloaking aliens.

“A more focused sequel that trades freedom for cinematic intensity.”

Crysis 2 takes a very different direction from the original. Instead of large open jungle sandboxes, it moves the action into a dense, destroyed New York City—and that change defines the entire experience.

The nanosuit returns, but it feels more streamlined and combat-oriented. You still have stealth, armor, and power modes, but the game encourages more direct confrontation compared to the experimental freedom of the first Crysis. It’s less about sandbox creativity and more about structured encounters.

Visually, it was ahead of its time when it launched. Even today, the city environments, lighting, and alien invasion set pieces hold up surprisingly well. The atmosphere of a collapsing New York is consistently strong and cinematic.

The story is more linear and character-driven this time. While it’s not particularly deep, it keeps a steady pace and does a good job pushing you through set-piece moments. However, it lacks some of the mystery and open-ended feel of the original.

The biggest change—and most divisive—is the reduced sandbox design. Levels are more corridor-like, and player freedom is noticeably limited. Some players will appreciate the tighter pacing, while others will miss the experimentation of the first game.

Pros:

Strong cinematic presentation
Excellent visuals and atmosphere
Improved combat pacing
More focused gameplay structure

Cons:

Reduced sandbox freedom
More linear level design
Less depth in gameplay experimentation

Verdict:
A solid sequel that shifts the series toward a more cinematic FPS direction. Not as free as Crysis 1, but still a very enjoyable experience.

My biggest problem with this game is just how unbalanced it feels (granted, I played it on post-human warrior) in both combat, and stealth. Let me elaborate on this by making comparisons to Crysis 1.

Obviously, the best thing to do during loud combat is to put your suit into armour mode. In Crysis 1, it worked like you'd expect. The energy bar essentially gave you another bar of health, and of course drained as you took damage. Why am I stating the obvious here? Because in Crysis 2, some genius thought it would be a good idea for it to drain your energy overtime, giving you less protection. And because you have WAY less health than in the first game, this feels like an unfair choice. Yeah, I could disable it while behind cover, but I didn't have to before, so why change it now? And even then, a stray shot or one flanking enemy could completely destroy me while my armour mode is off.

Further compounding this issue is how sprinting drains your energy too. In the first Crysis, sprinting only drained your energy while you were cloaked, or in speed mode (which made you incredibly fast). In Crysis 2, it'll drain your energy no matter what mode you're in.

"Isn't that in most games? Sprint stamina?" Well, yes it is. And that's fine, I guess. But here's the big problem: remember what I said about armour? In a nutshell, having both armour and sprint linked to the same damn bar can create this catch 22 situation that I can't say I've seen before elsewhere:

Say you're in combat, and you're taking a bit of a beating. You're on, say 30% energy. You gotta take cover. So you run towards the cover... but simply having armour mode on (and likely getting shot) saps your remaining energy, so now you're moving at a snail's pace, with the durability of a Pringle. What I'm getting at is, [b]running towards cover (which should save you) can put you in EVEN MORE DANGER.[/b] Maybe I'm playing the game wrong, but what worked in Crysis 1, should work in the damn sequel. Hell, what works in most FPSs should work in this.

Secondly, the balancing in stealth is a fucking joke. In Crysis 1, shooting any weapon while cloaked would instantly drain your energy to 0%, so you had to be careful with your timing. At best, you could quickly switch to another mode, shoot the dude, then cloak back, retaining most of your energy, but you had a slight risk of maybe switching to the wrong mode. In short, I say that worked. What does Crysis 2 do? Shooting a silenced weapon only drains like, 5% energy? And with how stupid the AI is when you're cloaked, as long as you're at the safe distance of 2 metres, a mook will watch thier friend die, and proceed to do nothing (or quickly get popped afterwards). Sure it's kinda funny, but it just makes stealth a joke. 

What gets me even more worked up are the stealth takedowns, as seen in most shooters with a stealth mechanic. First of all, you need to get so close to the enemy you run the risk of them noticing you on the spot. And sometimes, the prompt for the takedown disappears for no reason, so you end up slapping them, they notice you, and you die because you're a Pringle. And if you [i]do[/i] successfully trigger the takedown animation... you briefly uncloak... which can get you caught  (and this happened too many times to me). So... WHAT THE FUCK IS POINT OF TAKEDOWNS, IF JUST SHOOTING THEM IS EASIER [i]AND[/i] SAFER?!

Oh, and no FOV silder.

At the end of the day, I don't reccomend this game at all. If you must, just play the first Crysis (or frankly any other more interesting game). 4/10.
